text: What is the difference between factor income and transfer income?
options: Factor income is the income earned by factors of production, while transfer income is the income received by households as a result of transactions in the product market.
Transfer income is the income earned by factors of production, while factor income is the income received by households as a result of transactions in the product market.
Factor income and transfer income are the same thing.
Factor income is the income received by households as a result of transactions in the product market, while transfer income is the income earned by factors of production.
correctAnswer: Factor income is the income earned by factors of production, while transfer income is the income received by households as a result of transactions in the product market.
explanation: According to NCERT, factor income is the income earned by factors of production, such as wages, rent, interest, and profit. Transfer income, on the other hand, is the income received by households as a result of transactions in the product market, such as interest on savings or dividends on shares.

text: Which of the following is an example of an intermediate good?
options: A car manufactured by a company
A house purchased by a consumer
A computer chip used in the production of a smartphone
A smartphone purchased by a consumer
correctAnswer: A computer chip used in the production of a smartphone
explanation: According to NCERT, an intermediate good is a good that is used in the production of another good. In this case, the computer chip is an intermediate good because it is used in the production of a smartphone.

text: What is the formula for Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)?
options: $NFIA = X - M$
$NFIA = X + M$
$NFIA = X - IM$
$NFIA = X + IM$
explanation: According to NCERT, Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA) is calculated as the difference between the value of exports (X) and the value of imports (M). The formula is $NFIA = X - M$.

text: Which of the following is an example of an externality?
options: A factory emitting pollutants into the air
A consumer buying a product from a store
A farmer selling produce to a market
A student attending school
correctAnswer: A factory emitting pollutants into the air
explanation: According to NCERT, an externality is a cost or benefit that affects a third party who is not involved in the market transaction. In this case, the factory emitting pollutants into the air is an example of a negative externality because it affects the health and well-being of people living nearby.

text: Why is GDP not a perfect measure of welfare?
options: Because it does not take into account the distribution of income
Because it does not take into account the value of leisure time
Because it does not take into account the value of unpaid household work
All of the above
explanation: According to NCERT, GDP is not a perfect measure of welfare because it does not take into account the distribution of income, the value of leisure time, or the value of unpaid household work. These factors are important components of a person's overall well-being, but they are not included in the calculation of GDP.
